newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Lippo restructuring plan seen approved.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Lippo restructuring plan seen approved.

text.p: A controversial plan to restructure the financial subsidiaries of Indonesia's Lippo Group is likely to win shareholder approval despite misgivings, business analysts said on Thursday.

Analysts said shareholder meetings on Friday were likely to endorse the plan, which proposes an 875 billion rupiah ($380 million) chain of internal acquisitions between Lippo Life, Lippo Securities and Lippo Bank.

They said widespread criticism that the plan would allow the Riady family, which controls the diversified group, to cash in its shares had been at least partly allayed after Lippo deputy chairman James Riady announced a programme to sweeten the deal.

"My guess is that it will find shareholder approval," said William Keeling from Kleinwort Benson associate Mashill Securities. "But what we would deem essential is that any vote is seen to very firmly tie the Riady family into the group."
Lippo announced the massive restructuring plan early this month, under which Lippo Securities was to take an additional 27 percent stake in Lippo Life to raise its holding to 32 percent.
Lippo Life would then boost its holding in Lippo Bank to 45 percent with the purchase of an additional 40 percent stake.
The internal acquisitions, to be mostly funded by loans, will cut the Riadys' holding in the companies.
When the plan came in for sharp criticism from the business community, James Riady announced a reduction of the acquisition prices from a total of 902 billion rupiah to 875 billion rupiah.
He also said that any proceeds that the Riady family received through the restructuring would be ploughed back in a planned rights issue by Lippo Securities within 12 months.

In addition, he said the group would waive the 10 percent management fee on Lippo Bank's pre-tax earnings, irrespective of the outcome of the shareholder meetings. The amount involved is believed to be about 20 billion rupiah per year.
"It's a significant concession for the Riady family to make," said Keeling in a reference to the waiver. "It's a lot of money."
But analysts said they still were not entirely convinced of the need to restructure the companies.

"The impression I'm getting is that they have done enough to appease worries," said the head of a foreign brokerage in Jakarta. "We don't see as many negatives as before but we still don't see a huge amount of benefit."

"The market knows that they can get both votes through," said another foreign broker, referring to the shareholders' meeting at Lippo Securities to approve the Lippo Life purchase and a later Lippo Life meeting to endorse the Lippo Bank deal.
"The amount of cynicism among fund managers with regard to what's really going is still there. But the votes are going through, that is a fact," he added.
He said the Lippo management was taking pains to ensure a landslide vote approving the deal, and had bought almost all floating shares in Lippo Life to ensure the plan is endorsed.
"A mega pro-vote in Lippo Securities may be difficult to achieve because many small investors hold shares, but it is not completely out of the question," the broker added.

"A lot of local brokers hold proxies for small investors and the group is asking them to vote 'for'. All the locals I have spoken to are convinced that if they vote against the deal, they will suffer."
